```{r setup}
library(cystimap)
library(sf)
```

## Introduction

This vignette walks through the complete cystimap workflow using the
built-in North Carolina counties dataset (from the `sf` package) as a
stand-in study area, with a simulated point dataset representing case
counts. The same steps apply directly to a real epidemiological,
environmental, or ecological dataset.

## 1. Prepare the study area

Every cystimap workflow begins by defining the analytical environment:
coordinate reference system, boundary, and raster template. cystimap
never guesses a CRS — a projected CRS with linear units must be
supplied explicitly when a resolution is given.

```{r}
nc <- st_read(system.file("shape/nc.shp", package = "sf"), quiet = TRUE)

result <- prepare_study_area(
  boundary   = nc,
  crs        = 32119,      # NAD83 / North Carolina, metres
  resolution = 5000,       # 5km grid cells
  dissolve   = TRUE
)

print(result)
```

## 2. Read and prepare observation data

```{r}
set.seed(1)
n <- 40
dummy <- data.frame(
  id    = 1:n,
  lon   = runif(n, -80, -76),
  lat   = runif(n, 34, 36.5),
  cases = rpois(n, 10)
)
tmp_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
write.csv(dummy, tmp_file, row.names = FALSE)

result <- read_data(result, file = tmp_file, name = "cases")
```

## 3. Create an indicator, attach locations, and aggregate

`create_indicator()` combines what would otherwise be three separate
steps. The indicator formula is written naturally, without quoting.

```{r}
result <- create_indicator(
  result,
  data_name      = "cases",
  indicator_name = "case_rate",
  formula        = cases * 5,
  type           = "rate",
  coords         = c("lon", "lat"),
  coords_crs     = 4326
)

result$data$indicators$case_rate
```

## 4. Create a smooth spatial surface

cystimap supports Ordinary Kriging, IDW, Nearest Neighbour, and
existing-raster validation, all behind one consistent interface.

```{r}
result <- smooth_surface(
  result,
  indicator_name = "case_rate",
  surface_name   = "risk_surface",
  method         = "ordinary_kriging",
  mode           = "automatic",
  cv_method      = "loo"
)

result$surfaces$risk_surface$prediction
result$surfaces$risk_surface$cv_summary
```

Note the cross-validation summary above: because this example uses
randomly simulated data with no real spatial structure, correlation
is expected to be low. In a real analysis, this diagnostic should be
checked before interpreting the surface.

## 5. Classify the surface

```{r}
result <- classify_surface(
  result,
  surface_name    = "risk_surface",
  classified_name = "risk_binary",
  type            = "binary",
  cutoff_method   = "quantile",
  cutoffs         = 0.5
)

result$classified$risk_binary$frequencies
```

## 6. Combine classified surfaces

Combining requires two or more classified layers. Here we create a
second classification at a different threshold to demonstrate binary
overlap.

```{r}
result <- classify_surface(
  result,
  surface_name    = "risk_surface",
  classified_name = "risk_binary_q25",
  type            = "binary",
  cutoff_method   = "quantile",
  cutoffs         = 0.25
)

result <- combine_surfaces(
  result,
  classified_names = c("risk_binary", "risk_binary_q25"),
  combined_name    = "overlap",
  method           = "binary_overlap"
)

result$results$combined$overlap$frequencies
```

## 7. Scenarios: sensitivity, agreement, and consensus

The scenario framework generates every combination across
user-defined variable groups, executes each one, and evaluates how
much results change under different analytical assumptions.

```{r}
result <- define_scenarios(
  result,
  variable_groups = list(
    threshold_choice = c("risk_binary", "risk_binary_q25")
  ),
  combine_method = "binary_overlap"
)

result <- run_scenarios(result)
result <- scenario_sensitivity(result, outcome_value = 1, comparison = "pairwise")
result <- scenario_agreement(result)
result <- scenario_consensus(result, outcome_value = 1, min_scenarios = 1)

result$results$sensitivity
result$results$agreement
```

## 8. Administrative summaries

Any raster output can be summarised within polygons — here, North
Carolina counties.

```{r}
result <- admin_summary(
  result,
  raster_source = "surfaces", raster_name = "risk_surface",
  polygons = nc, zone_id = "NAME",
  stats = c("mean", "min", "max")
)

head(result$results$admin_summary$surfaces__risk_surface$summary_table)
```

## 9. Mapping

```{r}
map_surface(
  result,
  raster_source = "surfaces", raster_name = "risk_surface",
  title = "Simulated Case Rate Surface", legend_title = "Case Rate"
)
```

## 10. Export results

```{r, eval = FALSE}
export_results(result, output_dir = "my_analysis_output")
```

This writes all rasters, tables, the processing log, and a
reproducibility manifest to a tidy folder structure.

## Reproducibility

Every step above is recorded in `result$log`, giving a complete,
inspectable processing history:

```{r}
length(result$log)
result$log[[1]]$step
```

## Saving and restoring a cystimap object

Because `terra::SpatRaster` objects hold pointers to external memory,
ordinary `save()`/`saveRDS()` will not restore them safely across R
sessions. Use `save_cystimap()` / `load_cystimap()` instead:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
save_cystimap(result, "my_analysis.rds")
result <- load_cystimap("my_analysis.rds")
```
